newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's Verplaetse denies Italy/EMU report.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's Verplaetse denies Italy/EMU report.

text.p: Belgian central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse said on Tuesday he made no comments about Italy's possible membership of a future economic and monetary union (EMU) in a speech on Monday.

"I did not say that," he told Reuters when asked about a report in Belgian daily De Financieel Economische Tijd which quoted him as saying EMU would best start without Italy since the country will not be able to meet EMU entry criteria on budget deficits.

Verplaetse said he used the speech to talk about credible convergence plans, a strict adherence to the entry criteria and the sustainable character of measures which governments must take to meet the criteria. "But I made no allusion to Italy," he said.

"What I did say was that I favour an unimpaired adherence to the criteria, no toughening and no relaxing. I said that I hope as many countries as possible will join from the start (in 1999) and by 2001 all of them (EU members) will be in (EMU)."
"Large changes in government deficits in a year's time... I have questions about that," he said.

The paper had quoted Verplaetse as saying, "I would not mind seeing countries with a government deficit of seven percent (of gross domestic product) lowering their deficit to three percent in a year's time and in a durable way. In my view that is not possible." It concluded Verplaetse was speaking about Italy.
The paper said Italy had a budget deficit/GDP ratio of about seven percent in 1996 and aimed to cut the ratio to three percent in 1997 to be able to join EMU from the planned start.
The Maastricht Treaty sets a three percent deficit target for EU members to join EMU. Other criteria concern debt levels, and currency, interest rate and inflation stability.
Verplaetse told Reuters, "Three percent is sacred for Belgium...it is not up to me to have an opinion on Italy."

The paper said Verplaetse had doubts about an Italian plan to set a one-time tax to cut the deficit. "To raise taxes and promise that you partly pay them back next year...personally I feel a bit uneasy about that," it quoted him as saying.

Analysts have criticised the plan for being at odds with measures to achieve durable budget convergence between EU members, as outlined in the Maastricht Treaty. An EU ruling on various budgetary practices governments have used to bring deficits down to three percent of GDP is due later this week.
Financial markets are sceptical Italy and other Mediterranean countries have the track record to ensure a stable single currency, as desired by Germany in particular.

German public opinion insists the euro must be as solid as the mark. This means excluding from EMU countries such as Italy and Spain -- which have been better known for conducting inflationary policies than for their emphasis on stability.

Political leaders will choose the first group of nations to adopt the new currency early next year. It is largely expected to include a core of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg as well as a few others.
